title: The thunder glorifies
hook: the thunder glorifies His praise, and the angels too, in awe (13:13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'ibra, the lesson you cross over into. The story is the lesson.

A summer storm at night. The flash first, so bright the room goes white. Then you start counting, the way kids do: one, two, three. Then the sound, rolling across the roof, rattling the windows, so deep you feel it in your chest. Grown adults still flinch. Surah thirteen of the Qur'an is named for that sound. Ar-Ra'd: the thunder. And it hears something in that sound besides noise.

Verse twelve, in paraphrase: it is He who shows you the lightning, bringing fear and hope, and raises the heavy clouds. Fear of the strike, hope of the rain; for people in a dry land, both are real. Then verse thirteen, in Pickthall's translation: "The thunder hymneth His praise and (so do) the angels for awe of Him." The thunder isn't just a noise here. It's praising. The Qur'an says this in more than one place: another surah says there is nothing that doesn't glorify God with praise, but you don't understand their praise. Elsewhere it names the birds and the mountains among those that praise. Scholars read it in different ways. Some take it as real praise, in a language people can't follow. Some take it as the praise of a creature simply being what it was made to be. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi describes thunder as an angel charged with the clouds, and scholars discuss the strength of that report. Imam Malik records that 'Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr, a companion, would stop talking when he heard thunder, and say: glory be to the One whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels, in awe of Him. Some Muslims still say his words during a storm. A frightening sound, heard as praise, and a conversation paused out of respect, the way talk stops when someone nearby starts to pray.
screen: `LIGHTNING: FEAR AND HOPE.` · `THE THUNDER HYMNS HIS PRAISE.` · `ALL THINGS GLORIFY.` · `IBN AZ-ZUBAYR STOPS TALKING.` · then, large: `THE THUNDER IS PRAISING.`

segments.voice: Listen to whatever sound is around you: rain or wind if you have it, or traffic, a fan, the hum of a fridge. Don't name it; just listen, the way you'd listen to someone praying in another room. If you pray, you can say Ibn az-Zubayr's words, or simply subhanallah, glory be to God.
Ar-Ra'd. The surah named for the thunder: verse thirteen says it hymns God's praise, and the angels too, in awe.
Your line: the thunder is praising. A loud sound, heard another way. That's day four hundred forty-two.

original.note: Arabic: "the thunder," the name of Surah 13.

trapdoor: what you thought: thunder is just a loud noise.
what it means: in ar-Ra'd, the thunder is praising God, and the angels with it, in awe.

what a scholar hears: 13:13 echoes 17:44 (all things glorify Him); scholars differ on whether that praise is literal or the praise of a thing's being; Muwatta reports Ibn az-Zubayr's words at thunder.

chat.says: Why do some Muslims stop talking when it thunders?
options: A companion did: he paused to praise the One the thunder praises.
Because talking during a storm is forbidden in Islamic law.
Because the Qur'an orders silence whenever any storm comes.
chat.meaning: Malik records that 'Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr stopped talking at thunder and glorified the One whom the thunder glorifies with praise.
